description: Team of UNSW engineering students in Sydney. Grayson (Mechatronic / Robotic Engineering) is passionate about closing the bridge between space and learning and building technical applications with real-world impact. Shelley (Mechanical / Biomedical Engineering) is a research assistant applying CNNs to terahertz imaging data, and is passionate about bridging real-world experiences with emerging technology to solve practical problems. Together, we tackle the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.
summary:
Project LUNA is an intuitive mission-planning interface that allows users to compare and evaluate predetermined lunar south-pole landing sites across various temporal conditions. After selecting a location and landing date, the platform models the relative positions of the Sun and Earth against surrounding lunar terrain and utilises self-formulated physics models to estimate solar energy availability, battery performance and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

The platform was designed for ease-of-comparison between complex environmental constraints and making them accessible to mission planners, educators and the community. A TypeScript simulation engine forms its skeleton, accessible through a browser interface, HTTP API and command-line utility, allowing for consistent, reproducible outputs and detailed scenario analysis.

NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA elevation models were utilised to derive moon terrain data, while solar and terrestrial ephemerides were calculated using publicly accessible NASA NAIF SPICE kernels, independently validated against JPL Horizons.

LUNA addresses a significant challenge of polar exploration: low solar elevation angles make conditions highly dependent on local topography and landing date, where even small variations in terrain elevation influence available sunlight and mission viability. LUNA is intended as an educational and early-stage analytical tool, rather than a fully-certified mission-planning system.
details:
Project Background

Project LUNA began with two students who were enthusiastic about lunar exploration but had little prior experience with planetary ephemerides or terrain-based illumination modelling. Our first horizon reconstruction produced an almost flat lunar surface that omitted the craters, massifs and ridges dominating the south polar region, which made clear the scale of the problem we had undertaken.

Over the following days, much of our effort went into acquiring high-resolution elevation data and correcting errors in our visibility calculations. A recurring question was whether the Sun had set below the true horizon or was obscured by distant terrain. In most cases the cause was distant topography, often a crater rim hundreds of kilometres away.

This process showed us that our difficulties reflected a wider problem in polar mission planning. At the lunar south pole, small variations in local terrain can determine the solar power available to a lander, its opportunities to communicate with Earth and, ultimately, the viability of the mission. These relationships are difficult to assess without suitable analytical tools, and LUNA was developed to make them visible and quantifiable.

Why did we select the horizon?

 

Near the lunar poles the Sun never rises more than a few degrees above the horizon, so the local terrain horizon governs most of the power and communications budget.

The depth of a ridge and the timing of a landing both affect whether a spacecraft survives. LUNA computes the horizon from NASA elevation data, positions the Sun and Earth against it, and runs the energy and link models within a single engine.

 

Terrain horizon

LRO LOLA elevation models are sorted into four tiers of 5, 20, 40 and 120 m per pixel. For each azimuth, a ray follows the great circle over the curved Moon out to 300 km, samples the finest tier that covers each point, and keeps the maximum elevation angle (equation 1). The step is the larger of half a pixel and 0.2 % of range, so the ray does not skip nearby crests and still reaches the distant massifs that often set the polar horizon. With no terrain, the horizon is the smooth-sphere dip (equation 2).

Sun, Earth and ephemeris

We used SpiceyPy, DE440 and the lunar orientation kernels to build a table of Sun, Earth and Moon rotation at three-hour intervals from 2024 to 2040. The engine interpolates it with four-point Lagrange, so it never makes a live query. Bodies are discs of angular radius ρ (equation 3). The visible fraction is an area-weighted sum over nine Gauss-Chebyshev chords against the horizon (equation 4), and Earth eclipsing the Sun is handled as a circle overlap.

Architecture

The engine is pure TypeScript with no file or network access; hosts load the generated data and pass it in, so the Web Worker, the Hono API (18 endpoints) and the Luna CLI return identical numbers. The analysis layer sweeps dates, compares sites, builds year calendars and writes Markdown reports that name their terrain source.

Application

The explorer displays the terrain from orbit and from the lander, with the real horizon shown as a silhouette, the Sun at its true angular size and Earth in its current phase. The analysis page compares landing dates and sites and plots Sun visibility, battery charge and link availability for each date. All screenshots were taken from the running application.

Validation

An independent Python suite re-derives the models from the written specification rather than the engine source, and the table reports the misses alongside the matches. Compared with the literature, the most likely causes of disagreement are published coordinates rounded to about 300 m when sunlight varies by tens of points within 250 m, observer height (2 m against 10 m shifts a ridge result by 3 to 43 points), and the smoother 60 to 120 m LOLA grids used in earlier work. The 400 m browser preview terrain consistently overestimates ridge sunlight, by 4 to 37 points, and results computed on it are flagged accordingly.

The calendar, delay, compare, sensitivity, uncertainty, insights, report, API and CLI modules are covered by unit tests only. The models do not include relay satellites, nutation or polar motion. Near grazing sunrise, a small horizon error can shift event times by several minutes.

Benefits, impact and creativity

LUNA provides an initial comparison of landing sites and dates that runs in a web browser, without specialist software or live ephemeris queries. The visualisation and the numerical results come from the same engine and therefore cannot disagree, and every report identifies its terrain source.

LUNA is intended to help users ask better questions early about where and when to land near the south pole, before detailed mission tools are introduced. It also offers a clear way to teach why sunlight and Earth contact are difficult to secure at the poles.

The project's main creative contribution is treating the terrain horizon as the central object: a single curve that links lunar topography and orbital geometry to spacecraft survival. Discrepancies with published work are reported alongside the agreements, so uncertainty forms part of the result.

AI as an accelerator

Most of the code and documentation were written by Claude (Anthropic) using Claude Code. A planning session produced briefs, which coding subagents implemented against a binding specification. The team originated the core ideas, selected the questions, design direction and data, and determined what counts as validated. Validators were derived from the specification and kept independent of the code they test. Correctness rests on the tests and the comparisons above rather than on the model. No images, video or audio were generated by AI, and every number is computed by the deterministic engine from NASA data.

TypeScript, React, three.js, Hono and Web Workers; Python, SpiceyPy, Rasterio and Numba; Vitest and pytest.
